Notes from researching "the Merton equation" and "Jim Simons' theory" (Oct 2026), and whether they are still relevant to trading. The formulas themselves are in trading_equations.md.

1. "The Merton equation" — Robert C. Merton (Nobel 1997)

People usually mean one of these:

NameWhat it saysFormula
Black–Scholes–MertonPrice an option from a hedged stock + cash mix; the price depends on volatility, not on expected direction$C = S\,N(d_1) - K e^{-rT} N(d_2)$ (see equation 13)
Merton portfolio problemHow much of your wealth to keep in stocks$\pi^* = (\mu - r)/(\gamma\sigma^2)$; with γ = 1 it's continuous Kelly (equation 7)
Merton credit modelA company's equity is a call option on its assets, with the debt as strike → estimates default risk—
Merton jump-diffusionBlack–Scholes plus sudden price jumps—

Still relevant?

  • Black–Scholes: yes, as the market's common language, not as truth. Every option chain (NSE included) shows implied volatility and Greeks computed from it. Traders run it backwards to turn prices into IV and compare options by that. Its constant-volatility assumption is wrong: real markets show a volatility smile/skew — a study of Nifty options found a U-shaped smile. Desks extend it with Heston (stochastic volatility), jump-diffusion and local volatility.
  • Merton/Kelly sizing: very relevant. Professional trend-following funds use volatility targeting, which a 2026 paper describes as fractional Kelly. Practitioners use ¼–½ of Kelly because edge estimates are noisy and over-betting is far more costly than under-betting.

2. "Jim Simons' theory" — Renaissance Technologies / Medallion fund

  • There is no published Simons equation. Viral "Simons equation" posts often show the Chern–Simons form, which is geometry/physics, not markets.
  • What's publicly known (mostly from Zuckerman's The Man Who Solved the Market; Renaissance has never disclosed its methods):
    • First recruit Leonard Baum co-created the Baum–Welch algorithm for hidden Markov models (estimating hidden states from observed data).
    • Peter Brown and Robert Mercer joined in 1993 from IBM's HMM-based speech-recognition team.
    • Strategies are described as statistical arbitrage, pattern recognition and high-frequency trading; no primary source confirms the exact models used today.
  • The idea in one line: small statistical edge × huge number of independent bets × careful sizing. Expected profit ≈ N × (p·avg win − (1−p)·avg loss); with p only slightly above 50% but N in the millions, results become very reliable.
  • What an individual can use: HMM regime detection (trending vs choppy, calm vs volatile) as a filter on existing strategies (equation 17). The real edge — data, infrastructure, execution — isn't copyable.

3. Other models worth knowing (and how relevant)

AreaModelRelevance for a retail NSE trader
PerformanceSharpe, Sortino, max drawdownEssential — put in every backtest
PerformanceCAPM (Sharpe/Lintner), Fama–French 3-factorUseful — separates skill (alpha) from market exposure (beta). Fama & French (2004) say CAPM's empirical record is poor, but it's still widely used
SizingKelly / fractional Kelly / vol targetingEssential
VolatilityGARCH(1,1)Useful for forecasting volatility from returns
VolatilityHeston stochastic volatilityStandard for fitting option prices and the smile; only needed for options work
Mean reversionOrnstein–Uhlenbeck + cointegration (Avellaneda & Lee 2010 stat-arb)Useful — opens up pairs trading, a different edge from indicators
ExecutionAlmgren–ChrissKnow it exists — needs large orders
Market makingAvellaneda–StoikovKnow it exists — needs tick data and fast infrastructure

4. Applied to my own backtests (projects/trading experiments/)

Best Tori trendline result: daily, Break setup, 51.5% win rate, 2R target.

  • Expectancy = 0.515 × 2 − 0.485 = 0.545R per trade before costs.
  • Full Kelly = 0.515 − 0.485/2 ≈ 27% of capital at risk per trade — far too aggressive because the win rate is an estimate and costs/slippage lower it. Quarter Kelly (~7%) is still above the usual 1–2%.
  • Lesson: costs, slippage and honest edge estimates decide the outcome — the same thing the backtests showed.

5. Where my books cover this (books/ML/)

The library covers the statistics side, not the finance formulas:

  • HMMs (the Simons angle): Bishop PRML ch.13 pdf p625 · Murphy ML: A Probabilistic Perspective ch.17 pdf p620 · AIMA ch.14 pdf p474
  • Kalman filters / state-space (dynamic hedge ratios for pairs): Murphy Probabilistic Perspective ch.18 pdf p662
  • Grimes Art and Science of Trading (course workbook) (books/trading/): ch.11 quant tools pdf p412, ch.16 quantitative evidence pdf p546

Gap: nothing on Black–Scholes, GARCH or OU. Good additions: Hull, Options, Futures and Other Derivatives; Ernest Chan, Algorithmic Trading (mean reversion, Kelly, practitioner-focused).
